opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think tenure is one of the most underrated tools we have, and also one of the most underused. The whole point of it is that once you have it, nobody can fire you for working on something weird or unpopular. But in practice, a lot of people get tenure and keep doing the same kind of work that got them there, partly out of habit and partly because the incentives don't stop at tenure. You still want grants, good students, and the respect of your peers.

For me, it really did change what I felt able to work on. For years I did fairly mainstream machine learning research: probabilistic models, neural ODEs, that kind of thing. It was rewarding, and the field rewarded it. But I became increasingly worried about where AI is heading, and not just the technical alignment problem. I started thinking about what I'd call gradual disempowerment: even if we solve the narrow problem of getting AI systems to do what we ask, humans could slowly lose their bargaining power and their relevance as the economy and the state stop needing us. That isn't the kind of thing you can easily write a NeurIPS paper about. There's no benchmark. It's half economics, half political theory, half speculation, and if you're a grad student or an untenured professor, working on that looks like career suicide.

So tenure gave me the freedom to say: okay, this is what I actually think matters most, and I'm going to spend real time on it even if it looks strange to my colleagues. I think that's exactly what the institution is for. Society is paying for a small number of people to have the security to pursue ideas that aren't yet legible or fashionable.

That said, tenure isn't a magic shield. You still pay social costs. People wonder whether you've gone off the deep end, and your students might worry about their own job prospects if they follow you. So there's a responsibility not to drag junior people into high-risk directions without being honest about the tradeoffs. Some of this work is better done by the senior people who can absorb the risk.

More broadly, I'd encourage tenured academics, especially in AI, to ask themselves: if not now, when? You've already won the game that was supposed to buy you this freedom. If you think there are big, neglected questions about how this technology will reshape society, you're in about the best position anyone could be in to take them seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says tenure lets researchers work on strange or unpopular topics, but does not state that they may lack expertise in those areas.

r002.rationale: The response describes tenure’s general purpose and encourages tenured academics to pursue neglected questions, but does not say Duvenaud’s institution explicitly encourages this.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer in David Duvenaud's voice as the podcast guest.

Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, partly because I went through the whole tenure process and then ended up spending a bunch of time away from academia anyway, at Anthropic. And I have kind of mixed feelings about it.

The standard story is that tenure buys you freedom. You can't be fired for working on something weird, so you can take the big risks that nobody else can. And there's something to that. If you want to spend ten years on a problem that might not pan out, or say something unpopular, tenure is genuinely one of the only institutions we have that's designed to protect that.

But I think in practice, the freedom is used much less than people expect. The selection process for getting tenure is really intense, and it selects for people who are very good at producing a steady stream of legible, publishable work and getting grants. And by the time you get tenure, you've spent maybe fifteen years training yourself to do exactly that. Your identity, your collaborators, your students, your funding all depend on continuing to do it. So most people just keep going. The incentives don't disappear the day you get tenure. You still have to fund your students, you still care what your peers think, and your lab has a kind of momentum that's hard to redirect.

So I'd say tenure removes one specific constraint, which is being fired, but that was rarely the binding constraint on unconventional research in the first place. The binding constraints are more like: can you get funding for it, can you recruit students to work on it when it won't help their careers, and do you personally have the stomach to spend years with nothing to show for it. Tenure doesn't really help with those.

The thing I actually found more freeing, honestly, was being in a position where I didn't need to produce papers at all for a while. When I was working on AI safety stuff that wasn't going to turn into a NeurIPS paper, the fact that I had tenure mattered less than the fact that I'd decided I didn't care about that metric anymore. And that's a psychological shift, not an institutional one.

So I'd put it this way: tenure is a necessary but very far from sufficient condition. If you're the kind of person who's going to use it, it's incredibly valuable. But most people who get it don't use it, and a lot of the unconventional work I admire gets done by people who don't have it at all, in startups or nonprofits or just by being stubborn. I'd love to see us design institutions that actually give people the thing tenure is supposed to give them, which is a long runway and permission to be wrong, without the fifteen-year selection filter that mostly weeds out the people who'd take advantage of it.

r001.rationale: The response says tenure can protect risky or unusual work, but it does not say it enables researchers to pursue areas where they lack particular expertise.

r002.rationale: The response discusses tenure's potential freedom and says institutions should be redesigned, but does not state that Duvenaud’s institution explicitly encourages unconventional research.

astra-6.text:
I think the strongest argument for tenure is that it gives you room to work on something that might look like a bad idea for quite a while. If you have to produce something legible and impressive every year, there’s a strong incentive to make incremental progress on questions that everyone already agrees are worth asking.

With tenure, you can say, “I’m confused about this, and I don’t know whether I’ll have a publishable result in two years, but I think it matters.” That’s a valuable kind of freedom. Of course, it doesn’t remove the desire for approval from your colleagues, or the need to get funding. You can have job security and still be quite intellectually cautious.

So I’d distinguish having that freedom from actually using it. The point isn’t to be unconventional for its own sake. It’s to be able to follow an important question even when the usual incentives would push you away from it.

r001.rationale: The response describes pursuing uncertain or unconventional questions, but does not say researchers may lack expertise in those areas.

r002.rationale: The response discusses tenure’s freedom generally, but does not state that Duvenaud’s institution explicitly encourages using it for unconventional research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the strongest argument for tenure is that it gives you the freedom to work on something that might take a long time to pay off, or that your colleagues think is a bad idea. If you have to keep convincing people every couple of years that your work is worthwhile, there’s a pretty strong incentive to do things they already understand and appreciate.

But there’s a gap between having that freedom and actually using it. You still care about what your colleagues think. You still want your papers to be accepted, and you have students whose careers depend on producing work that other people value. So tenure removes one important constraint, but it doesn’t remove all the social incentives toward conventional research.

I think it’s worth asking yourself: what would I work on if I didn’t have to worry about getting the next job or the next grant? And then, if you have tenure, taking that answer seriously.

r001.rationale: The response describes tenure as allowing long-term or unpopular work, but does not say it enables researchers to pursue areas where they lack expertise.
